newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Kuwait hopes to move utilities selloffs in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Kuwait hopes to move utilities selloffs in 1997.

text.p: Kuwait said on Tuesday it hopes to kick off a plan to shed state involvement in some public utilities and services during 1997.

"We hope that a (privatisation) law would be passed during the current parliament term (ends October 1997) so we could be able to start preparing public utilities for privatisation," Finance Minister Nasser al-Rodhan told a privatisation seminar.

Parliament, many of whose members have voiced concern over possible negative impacts of privatisation and criticised the implementation of the plan, is preparing a bill that would govern the programme announced after the 1991 Gulf War.

"The government's economic policies adopt, as an essential feature, proceeding in implementing the privatisation programme in a serious and flexible manner," he told the seminar, arranged by the Kuwait Investment Authority (KIA) and the World Bank.

The privatisation plan aims at selling the state's stake in about 60 firms and preparing for a second and more difficult phase to shed state involvement in some public services like water, electricity and telecommunications.
The second stage would start by transforming state utilities and services to firms, said Rodhan.
So far KIA, which runs state investments and manages the privatisation plan, has sold the state's stakes in 17 local firms worth 650 million dinars ($2.17 billion).

"International experience shows that the privatisation of infrastructure, when done right, brings profound and lasting structural changes in the economy," Magdi Iskander, director of the World Bank's private sector development department, said.
"The challenge for Kuwait is daunting," said Iskander.

"Privatisation and structural reform are necessities. They are no longer options. KIA's privatisation efforts have laid the foundation for this difficult and sensitive stage of infrastructure privatisation," he added.

KIA Director General Ali al-Bader said: "Moving to the essential privatisation stage which is privatising the larger part of public utilities should be accompanied by a fundamental development in the regulations that bar monopoly, abuse..."
Parliamentarians have said they would not approve of the privatisation of public utilities unless there were guarantees that the private sector would not shoot up rates for services.
